title: Arts in the Age of Data: skills tree
intro: Tick the skills you've learned on the unit. As you go, the tree fills in, and the read-out below turns what you've done into language you can use in CVs, applications and interviews.

themes.label: Digital and technical skills
themes.blurb: Confident use of the software employers expect, from spreadsheets to visual analytics.

themes.label: Research and data gathering
themes.blurb: Finding, judging and assembling information from many kinds of source.

themes.label: Analytical and numerical reasoning
themes.blurb: Working with numbers carefully to find and test patterns.

themes.label: Critical thinking and ethical judgement
themes.blurb: Asking where data comes from, what it leaves out and what it really shows.

themes.label: Communicating with data
themes.blurb: Turning analysis into charts and writing that a non-specialist can follow.

themes.label: Teamwork and leadership
themes.blurb: Working with others to deliver a shared piece of work.

themes.label: Project management and organisation
themes.blurb: Planning, organising and delivering a project from question to finished output.

nodes.label: Excel User L1
nodes.cv: Organised, cleaned and formatted data in Excel using tables, filters, sorting and formulae with relative and absolute references.
nodes.story: Think of a time a spreadsheet you inherited or built was messy or unreliable. What did you do to make it usable, and how did you check it was right?
nodes.next: Practise the keyboard shortcuts until they are automatic: speed and accuracy in Excel are noticed in almost any office role.

nodes.label: Relative & fixed references
nodes.desc: Use $ signs so formulae copy correctly across rows and columns.

nodes.label: Cell references
nodes.desc: Point formulae at the right cells and ranges.

nodes.label: Simple formulae
nodes.desc: Write basic calculations: add, subtract, multiply, divide.

nodes.label: Selection shortcuts
nodes.desc: Move and select large ranges quickly with the keyboard.

nodes.label: Load and Save
nodes.desc: Open, save and keep track of versions of your workbooks.

nodes.label: Paste special
nodes.desc: Paste values, formats or transposed data rather than everything.

nodes.label: Filters
nodes.desc: Show only the rows you need.

nodes.label: Using Sheets
nodes.desc: Organise a workbook across several named sheets.

nodes.label: Tables
nodes.desc: Turn a range into an Excel Table that grows and formats itself.

nodes.label: Set data types
nodes.desc: Make sure numbers, dates and text are stored as the right type.

nodes.label: Format a cell
nodes.desc: Control number formats, alignment and borders.

nodes.label: Find and Replace
nodes.desc: Fix repeated errors and inconsistencies in one go.

nodes.label: Sort
nodes.desc: Order data by one or more columns.

nodes.label: Excel User L2
nodes.cv: Used lookup, conditional and summary functions (VLOOKUP, IF, SUMIF and COUNTIF) and pivot tables to combine and summarise datasets in Excel.
nodes.story: When did you need an answer the raw data didn't give you directly? Which formulae or pivot tables did you use to get there?
nodes.next: Learn XLOOKUP and INDEX/MATCH, which many workplaces now use in place of VLOOKUP.

nodes.label: V-Lookups
nodes.desc: Pull matching values from one table into another.

nodes.label: Text functions
nodes.desc: Split, join and tidy text with functions such as LEFT, TRIM and CONCAT.

nodes.label: Dropdown
nodes.desc: Use data validation lists to control what can be entered.

nodes.label: IF conditions
nodes.desc: Make formulae that return different results depending on a test.

nodes.label: SUMIF, COUNTIF, AVERAGEIF
nodes.desc: Total, count or average only the rows that meet a condition.

nodes.label: Pivot tables
nodes.desc: Summarise large tables by category in a few clicks.

nodes.label: Convert data format
nodes.desc: Move data between formats such as .csv and .xlsx without losing anything.

nodes.label: Excel User L3
nodes.cv: Built interactive Excel outputs with pivot charts, slicers and conditional formatting, and used tools such as Go To Special and Text to Columns to restructure data quickly.
nodes.story: Describe something you built in Excel that other people could use without your help. How did you make it easy for them?
nodes.next: Build a one-page interactive Excel dashboard from your project data and keep it as a portfolio piece.

nodes.label: Pivot Graphs
nodes.desc: Chart directly from a pivot table.

nodes.label: Conditional formatting
nodes.desc: Highlight cells automatically by rule, such as colour scales.

nodes.label: Slicers
nodes.desc: Add clickable filters to pivot tables and charts.

nodes.label: Goto special
nodes.desc: Select blanks, formulae or errors across a sheet at once.

nodes.label: Text to columns
nodes.desc: Split one column into several at a delimiter.

nodes.label: Specialist Technical Skills
nodes.cv: Used Power Query and calculated pivot fields to automate data preparation and analysis in Excel.
nodes.story: Tell me about a repetitive data task you automated. How much time did it save, and how did you make sure it was reliable?
nodes.next: Try Power BI, which uses the same Power Query engine and is widely used in business and the public sector.

nodes.label: Calculated pivot fields
nodes.desc: Add your own calculations inside a pivot table.

nodes.label: Power Query
nodes.desc: Import, clean and join data with repeatable steps.

nodes.label: Tableau User L1
nodes.cv: Imported data into Tableau and built charts using measures, dimensions and the Marks card.
nodes.story: Why did you choose Tableau rather than Excel for a particular chart, and what difference did it make?
nodes.next: Publish a chart to a free Tableau Public profile and link it from your CV or LinkedIn.

nodes.label: Basic Formatting
nodes.desc: Format titles, axes and labels in Tableau.

nodes.label: Tableau Charts
nodes.desc: Build standard chart types in Tableau.

nodes.label: Import data into Tableau
nodes.desc: Connect Tableau to Excel or .csv data.

nodes.label: Tableau Markers
nodes.desc: Use the Marks card for colour, size, labels and detail.

nodes.label: Measures, dimension, attributes
nodes.desc: Know how Tableau treats categories and numbers.

nodes.label: Tableau User L2
nodes.cv: Created interactive Tableau dashboards, maps and stories, joining multiple datasets and exporting presentation-ready graphics.
nodes.story: Walk me through a dashboard you built. Who was it for, and what did you want them to be able to find out for themselves?
nodes.next: Tableau offers entry-level certifications if you want a formal credential to put on your CV.

nodes.label: Advanced Formatting
nodes.desc: Fine-tune design across a whole workbook.

nodes.label: Joining datasets
nodes.desc: Combine tables with joins and relationships.

nodes.label: Export images
nodes.desc: Export charts at a quality fit for reports.

nodes.label: Story boards
nodes.desc: Sequence views into a Tableau Story.

nodes.label: Interactive Tableaus
nodes.desc: Build dashboards with filters and actions.

nodes.label: Tableau Maps
nodes.desc: Plot data geographically in Tableau.

nodes.label: Data Gatherer
nodes.cv: Located, assessed and extracted data from published reports and official sources, converting it into analysis-ready formats.
nodes.story: Describe how you tracked down the data your project needed. What did you do when it wasn't in the form you wanted?
nodes.next: Get to know the main UK sources (ONS, data.gov.uk, the UK Data Service) so you know where to look first in any new role.

nodes.label: Data search
nodes.desc: Find suitable datasets for a question.

nodes.label: Extract report table
nodes.desc: Lift tables out of published reports into a spreadsheet.

nodes.label: Download .xlsx data
nodes.desc: Download and open published Excel datasets.

nodes.label: Data Creator
nodes.cv: Created new datasets by digitising printed or visual sources, assembling time series from several releases and pulling custom extracts from online databases.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time the data you needed didn't exist yet. How did you build it, and how did you check its accuracy?
nodes.next: Digitise a small archival or historical source of your own: it makes a strong portfolio piece for research, heritage and archive roles.

nodes.label: Web database extracts
nodes.desc: Query an online database and download a custom extract.

nodes.label: Download .csv data
nodes.desc: Work with plain-text .csv downloads.

nodes.label: Create time series
nodes.desc: Assemble figures from several releases into one series over time.

nodes.label: Digitize data
nodes.desc: Turn printed tables, charts or archives into usable data.

nodes.label: Advanced Data Types
nodes.cv: Worked with non-standard data formats, including JSON, shapefiles, social-media and text data, and weighted survey data.
nodes.story: Describe a dataset that was harder to work with than a normal spreadsheet. What did you have to learn to use it?
nodes.next: An introductory Python or R course is the natural next step: these formats are where code starts to pay off.

nodes.label: Shapefile data
nodes.desc: Use geographic boundary files for mapping.

nodes.label: Twitter data
nodes.desc: Work with social-media posts as data.

nodes.label: Word counts data
nodes.desc: Turn text into counts you can analyse.

nodes.label: Weighted survey data
nodes.desc: Apply survey weights so results represent the population.

nodes.label: JSON data
nodes.desc: Read data in the nested JSON format used by many web sources.

nodes.label: Launch Data Project
nodes.cv: Scoped a group data project: chose a topic, defined the problem and research questions, decided what to measure and set up a project plan and shared workspace.
nodes.story: Tell me how your group chose its topic and turned it into a question data could answer. What trade-offs did you make?
nodes.next: Practise writing a one-paragraph project brief in plain English: it is how most workplace projects begin.

nodes.label: Backup procedures
nodes.desc: Keep safe copies so no work is lost.

nodes.label: Project space setup
nodes.desc: Set up a shared folder structure for the group.

nodes.label: Ask good data questions
nodes.desc: Frame questions that data can actually answer.

nodes.label: Team protocols
nodes.desc: Agree how the group will communicate and decide.

nodes.label: Defining a problem
nodes.desc: Turn a broad interest into a focused problem.

nodes.label: Team formation
nodes.desc: Form a group and get to know each other's strengths.

nodes.label: Briefed & Ready to Go
nodes.desc: Understand the brief and what success looks like.

nodes.label: Project plan
nodes.desc: Plan the stages, tasks and deadlines.

nodes.label: Topic selection
nodes.desc: Choose a topic with data available to support it.

nodes.label: What to measure
nodes.desc: Decide which indicators will answer your question.

nodes.label: Create a ZIP folder
nodes.desc: Package files for sharing and submission.

nodes.label: Wrangler
nodes.cv: Cleaned, structured and combined raw datasets, documenting sources and field definitions so the work could be checked and reused.
nodes.story: Describe a problem you found while cleaning data, such as missing values, inconsistent names or a misleading field. How did you spot it, and what did you do?
nodes.next: Keep a short data dictionary for every project: it is standard practice in analyst roles.

nodes.label: Discovery
nodes.desc: Explore a new dataset to see what it contains.

nodes.label: Structuring
nodes.desc: Reshape data into tidy rows and columns.

nodes.label: Cleaning
nodes.desc: Fix errors, gaps and inconsistencies.

nodes.label: Attribute sources
nodes.desc: Record where every dataset came from.

nodes.label: Field definitions
nodes.desc: Document what each column means.

nodes.label: Enrich & combine
nodes.desc: Join datasets to add new variables.

nodes.label: Advanced Wrangler
nodes.cv: Validated and integrated three or more datasets, managing storage and versions and checking combined results for consistency.
nodes.story: Tell me about combining several datasets. What went wrong when you joined them, and how did you find out?
nodes.next: A free introduction to SQL would show you how organisations manage data at scale.

nodes.label: Validate
nodes.desc: Check combined data for errors and mismatches.

nodes.label: Storing lots of data
nodes.desc: Manage large files and many versions.

nodes.label: Process 3 datasets
nodes.desc: Prepare and integrate three or more datasets.

nodes.label: Team player 1
nodes.cv: Contributed to a group project by taking on a defined role, recording action points, reporting progress and helping the group reach compromises.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time your group disagreed. What compromise did you reach, and what was your part in it?
nodes.next: Your group's weekly decision log is evidence: use specific entries from it as examples in applications and interviews.

nodes.label: Complete a shared task
nodes.desc: Finish a piece of work together.

nodes.label: Write up meeting action list
nodes.desc: Record who will do what by when.

nodes.label: Update on your progress
nodes.desc: Keep the group informed about your work.

nodes.label: Identify your role
nodes.desc: Know what you are responsible for in the group.

nodes.label: Make a compromise
nodes.desc: Find a way forward when views differ.

nodes.label: Team player 2
nodes.cv: Took responsibility for a distinct part of a team project, met agreed targets, and gave and acted on constructive feedback.
nodes.story: Describe a time you gave a teammate feedback, or acted on feedback you received. What changed as a result?
nodes.next: Ask a teammate for one specific piece of feedback about your contribution that you could quote or paraphrase in an application.

nodes.label: Ask for feedback from team
nodes.desc: Invite comments on your work.

nodes.label: Responsible part of team project
nodes.desc: Own a distinct part of the project.

nodes.label: Negotiate individual report focus
nodes.desc: Agree your individual angle within the group project.

nodes.label: Hit targets for agreed actions
nodes.desc: Deliver what you said you would, on time.

nodes.label: Offer constructive feedback
nodes.desc: Give useful, specific and kind feedback.

nodes.label: Leadership
nodes.cv: Helped lead a team: checked progress against the plan, supported colleagues, built agreement and led the response when things went wrong.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time a project went off track. How did you notice, and what did you do to bring the team back together?
nodes.next: Look for chances to lead beyond the unit, through societies, volunteering or a student representative role.

nodes.label: Help team member
nodes.desc: Support a colleague who is stuck.

nodes.label: Assess if team on track
nodes.desc: Check progress against the plan.

nodes.label: Consult on ways forward
nodes.desc: Gather views before deciding.

nodes.label: Generate group agreement
nodes.desc: Bring the group to a shared decision.

nodes.label: Action plan something going wrong
nodes.desc: Respond with a plan when things go off track.

nodes.label: All Round Data Hero
nodes.cv: Completed the full Arts in the Age of Data skills tree, across software, data sourcing, project management, teamwork, critical interpretation, analysis and visualisation.
nodes.story: If you had to pick one piece of work from this unit that shows what you can do, what would it be, and why?
nodes.next: Think about which strand you most enjoyed: it is a good clue to the kind of role to look for.

nodes.label: Age of Data Context
nodes.cv: Explored the historical and ethical context of data: how states and organisations came to count people, who holds power over data, and what that means for how it should be used.
nodes.story: Tell me about an ethical question you considered when working with data. How did it change what you did?
nodes.next: Find out how your target sector governs data, such as the basics of UK GDPR for any role that handles personal information.

nodes.label: Data ethics
nodes.desc: Weigh the ethical questions raised by collecting and using data.

nodes.label: Scale of data
nodes.desc: Understand how much data now exists and why that matters.

nodes.label: Origins of the Data State
nodes.desc: Know how and why states began counting their people.

nodes.label: Power and data
nodes.desc: Ask who controls data and who benefits.

nodes.label: Case studies
nodes.cv: Critically evaluated real-world statistics, polls and surveys, asking why the data exists, what it does and doesn't count, and how it can be spun.
nodes.story: Give an example of a statistic used in a misleading way. How did you work out what was really going on?
nodes.next: Keep this sharp by following fact-checking organisations and asking the same questions of the numbers you meet in the news.

nodes.label: What we choose to measure
nodes.desc: See that choosing a measure is itself a decision.

nodes.label: How to judge a survey
nodes.desc: Assess a survey's sample, questions and method.

nodes.label: How to read a poll
nodes.desc: Interpret polls, margins of error and headlines.

nodes.label: Society's common stats
nodes.desc: Know the everyday statistics that shape public debate.

nodes.label: How is data spun?
nodes.desc: Spot selective or misleading uses of data.

nodes.label: Why does this data exist?
nodes.desc: Ask who collected the data and for what purpose.

nodes.label: What is or isn't counted?
nodes.desc: Notice who and what is missing from a dataset.

nodes.label: Analyst
nodes.cv: Identified patterns in data, framed testable hypotheses, made assumptions explicit and explained clearly what the data does and does not show.
nodes.story: Tell me about a finding from your project. How confident were you in it, and how did you explain its limits?
nodes.next: Practise summarising a finding in one sentence for a non-specialist, then in one paragraph for an expert.

nodes.label: Data assumptions
nodes.desc: Make the assumptions behind your analysis explicit.

nodes.label: Generate hypothesis
nodes.desc: Propose an explanation you can test.

nodes.label: Clear explanations of what data shows
nodes.desc: Say plainly what the data does and does not show.

nodes.label: Identify patterns
nodes.desc: Spot trends, outliers and differences.

nodes.label: Data Humanist
nodes.cv: Interpreted findings with nuance, weighing alternative explanations and situating results within the relevant literature and the wider history of data.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time a finding turned out to be more complicated than it first looked. How did you explain that to others?
nodes.next: This is your distinctive edge as an arts, law or social sciences graduate: lead with it when applying for analytical roles.

nodes.label: Recognise alternative
nodes.desc: Consider other explanations for a finding.

nodes.label: Nuance
nodes.desc: Avoid overclaiming; acknowledge complexity.

nodes.label: Situate project in Age of Data
nodes.desc: Connect your project to the unit's wider themes.

nodes.label: Situate findings in topic literature
nodes.desc: Relate your results to what others have written.

nodes.label: Theory & history inform viz choices
nodes.desc: Let theory and history shape how you visualise.

nodes.label: What findings mean
nodes.desc: Explain why the results matter.

nodes.label: Analyst Foundations
nodes.cv: Calculated totals and percentages accurately and distinguished between categorical and numerical data before analysing them.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time a simple calculation mattered. How did you make sure it was right?
nodes.next: Many graduate employers use numerical reasoning tests: practise these alongside your project work.

nodes.label: Totalling
nodes.desc: Add up columns and groups accurately.

nodes.label: %s
nodes.desc: Calculate and interpret percentages.

nodes.label: Quick maths in Excel
nodes.desc: Do fast calculations with Excel.

nodes.label: Categorical data
nodes.desc: Work with data in categories.

nodes.label: Numerical data
nodes.desc: Work with data measured in numbers.

nodes.label: Summarise data
nodes.cv: Summarised datasets with averages, ranges, percentiles and frequency counts, choosing the right measure for the data.
nodes.story: When did choosing the median rather than the mean, or the reverse, change the story your data told?
nodes.next: Try summarising a public dataset in five numbers and two sentences: it is a common task in analyst interviews.

nodes.label: Mean, Median, Mode
nodes.desc: Choose the right average for the data.

nodes.label: Range & Percentiles
nodes.desc: Describe the spread of values.

nodes.label: Frequency counts
nodes.desc: Count how often each value occurs.

nodes.label: Compare datasets
nodes.cv: Compared datasets using measures of spread such as variance and standard deviation.
nodes.story: Tell me about two groups or places you compared. How did you decide whether the difference was meaningful?
nodes.next: Find out what a confidence interval is: it is the natural next step from standard deviation.

nodes.label: Standard deviation
nodes.desc: Measure how spread out values are.

nodes.label: Variance
nodes.desc: Measure spread as the average squared distance from the mean.

nodes.label: Change over time
nodes.cv: Measured change over time using percentage change, average growth, index numbers, inflation adjustment and trendlines.
nodes.story: Describe a trend you measured. How did you make sure you were comparing like with like across the years?
nodes.next: Use the ONS inflation calculators and indices to practise real-terms comparisons on topics you care about.

nodes.label: Index numbers
nodes.desc: Express values relative to a base year set to 100.

nodes.label: Avg. % growth
nodes.desc: Calculate average growth over several periods.

nodes.label: Adjusting for inflation
nodes.desc: Compare money values across years in real terms.

nodes.label: Trendlines
nodes.desc: Fit a line to show the direction of change.

nodes.label: % change
nodes.desc: Calculate the percentage change between two values.

nodes.label: Detect relationships
nodes.cv: Tested relationships between variables with scatter graphs and the correlation coefficient (r), and explained the difference between correlation and causation.
nodes.story: Tell me about a relationship you found in your data. How did you avoid claiming more than it showed?
nodes.next: Look for a correlation reported in the news and work out what else could explain it.

nodes.label: Scatter graphs
nodes.desc: Plot two variables against each other.

nodes.label: Correlation theory
nodes.desc: Know what correlation can and cannot tell you.

nodes.label: Finding R
nodes.desc: Calculate and interpret the correlation coefficient.

nodes.label: Causation
nodes.cv: Applied linear regression and contingency coefficients to explore causal questions, and assessed the limits of causal claims.
nodes.story: Tell me about a time you tried to establish cause and effect. What stopped you being certain?
nodes.next: An introductory statistics or quantitative methods course would build directly on this.

nodes.label: Contingency Coefficient
nodes.desc: Measure association between categorical variables.

nodes.label: Linear Regression
nodes.desc: Model how one variable changes with another.

nodes.label: Common visualisations
nodes.cv: Created clear column, line and pie charts, formatting axes, legends, colour and annotation for readability.
nodes.story: Show me a chart you improved. What did the default version get wrong, and what did you change?
nodes.next: Every time you make a chart, ask what you can remove: it is the quickest way to improve.

nodes.label: Add annotation
nodes.desc: Label the key points readers should notice.

nodes.label: Color features
nodes.desc: Use colour with purpose.

nodes.label: Remove features
nodes.desc: Strip out clutter from default charts.

nodes.label: Legends
nodes.desc: Add, place or replace legends.

nodes.label: Axis formatting
nodes.desc: Set scales, labels and number formats on axes.

nodes.label: Line graphs
nodes.desc: Show change over time.

nodes.label: Column charts
nodes.desc: Compare quantities across categories.

nodes.label: Pie charts
nodes.desc: Show parts of a whole, and know when not to.

nodes.label: Design principles
nodes.cv: Applied design principles, including audience, low-ink design and appropriate chart choice, to make visualisations clear and honest.
nodes.story: Tell me about designing something for a particular audience. How did knowing who they were change your choices?
nodes.next: Collect three charts you admire and three you don't, and write a line on why for each.

nodes.label: Audience
nodes.desc: Design for the people who will read it.

nodes.label: Low ink
nodes.desc: Remove everything that doesn't carry information.

nodes.label: Sparklines
nodes.desc: Show trends in a small, word-sized chart.

nodes.label: Histograms
nodes.desc: Show the distribution of a numerical variable.

nodes.label: Doughnut charts
nodes.desc: Use a ring chart for parts of a whole.

nodes.label: Infographic design
nodes.cv: Designed an infographic with a clear structure and flow, choosing chart types, including tree maps and radar charts, to fit the story.
nodes.story: Walk me through how you planned your infographic's layout. What did you put first, and why?
nodes.next: Keep a PDF of your infographic to share in applications and interviews.

nodes.label: Structure and flow
nodes.desc: Lead the reader through the page in a clear order.

nodes.label: Word Cloud
nodes.desc: Visualise word frequency in text.

nodes.label: Tree map
nodes.desc: Show nested parts of a whole as rectangles.

nodes.label: Radar chart
nodes.desc: Compare several measures on one chart.

nodes.label: Concise text
nodes.desc: Write short, precise text to go with charts.

nodes.label: Integrated report: text & data viz
nodes.cv: Produced an integrated report combining concise written analysis with data visualisations for a non-specialist audience.
nodes.story: Walk me through your final infographic. Who was it for, and what design and writing decisions did you make for them?
nodes.next: Rewrite your report's key message as a 100-word briefing note: a format used across government, policy and business.

nodes.label: Pyramid chart
nodes.desc: Compare two distributions back to back, such as by age and sex.

nodes.label: Area chart
nodes.desc: Show volume over time.

nodes.label: Advanced data viz storytelling
nodes.cv: Developed advanced data storytelling by studying the history of data visualisation, recreating landmark designs and avoiding distortion.
nodes.story: Tell me about a famous visualisation you studied or recreated. What did it teach you about your own work?
nodes.next: Build a small portfolio of two or three visualisations with a short note on each design choice.

nodes.label: Avoiding distortion
nodes.desc: Keep scales and shapes honest.

nodes.label: History of Data Viz
nodes.desc: Learn from landmark designs and designers.

nodes.label: Replicate famous design
nodes.desc: Rebuild a classic visualisation to learn how it works.

nodes.label: Find inspiration
nodes.desc: Collect and learn from good current work.

nodes.label: Mapping
nodes.cv: Created thematic maps of data at city, UK and global scales.
nodes.story: Tell me about a map you made. What did showing the data geographically reveal that a chart didn't?
nodes.next: If map-making appeals, try QGIS, which is free and used widely in government, planning and heritage.

nodes.label: UK
nodes.desc: Map data for the UK's nations and regions.

nodes.label: Thematic maps
nodes.desc: Shade areas by a variable (choropleth and similar).

nodes.label: Around the world
nodes.desc: Map data for countries worldwide.

nodes.label: Cities
nodes.desc: Map data within and across cities.
